3 ADULT BEETLES
For hundreds of millions of years,
the rules of the pond seemed simple.
If you are an amphibian with a
lightning-fast tongue, insects are food.
A frog sits, a bug moves,
and a sticky tongue ends the story.
But what if one bug has learned
to use that rule against the frog?
Today, we are meeting a beetle
that turns the hunter into the meal.
Imagine a damp bank near a shallow
pool, late at night.
A frog sits very still,
watching for movement.
A few inches away,
something small and pale is twitching.
It looks soft, slow, and defenseless.
To the frog, it looks like the
easiest meal of the week.
It is not.
It is a trap,
and the trap is alive.
Meet Epomis, a genus of ground beetles.
Ground beetles are common night hunters.
They run across soil and leaf
litter, and most of them eat small
prey like worms, snails, or caterpillars.
Nobody would expect one to take on a frog.
Yet Epomis larvae are different.
In the laboratory, they feed on
amphibians, and nothing else.
In 2011, researchers at Tel Aviv
University in Israel, Gil Wizen
and Avital Gasith, published the
first detailed study of this behavior.
They called it a role reversal:
the animal that should be the
predator becomes the prey.
To see how this works,
we first have to understand a frog's eyes.
A frog does not look at the
world the way you do.
Its visual system is tuned to catch
small moving things.
A tiny dark spot that twitches
is a signal that says, strike now.
This reflex has fed frogs for a
very long time.
Epomis has learned to push exactly
that button.
When a frog comes near,
the larva does not hide,
and it does not run.
It stays still and starts to move
its antennae and its jaws,
in a slow rhythm,
up and down and from side to side.
To us it might look like a tiny dance.
To a frog, it can look like
a worm, wriggling on the ground.
The researchers counted the movements.
When a toad was fifteen centimeters
away, the larva waved about three
times a minute.
When the toad was only one
centimeter away, the rate rose
to about five times a minute.
In control tests, with nothing
to lure, the larvae barely moved at all.
The larva was not just wiggling.
It was paying attention.
That control matters, because it
shows that the dance is not random shaking.
It changes with the distance to the victim.
A trap that gets more convincing
as the target gets closer is a
very clever trap.
Now the frog commits.
It turns its body toward the larva,
lowers its head, and creeps closer.
The larva does not flinch.
It keeps waving.
Then the frog strikes.
A frog's tongue can leave its mouth
in a fraction of a second,
far too fast for you to follow
with your eyes.
For almost any insect,
this is the end.
The tongue is wet and sticky,
it snaps back with the prey stuck
on it, and the meal is swallowed
before the insect understands what happened.
A frog that uses this weapon again
and again rarely misses a small,
wriggling target.
That is exactly why the larva's
trick is so shocking:
it survives the one move that almost
always works.
But in the Epomis experiments,
the larva usually avoids the tongue.
The authors write that it almost
always dodges the strike.
Then it does something no ordinary
insect would dare.
It uses the moment,
when the frog is open and close,
to grab on to the amphibian's body
with its hooked jaws.
Look closely at those jaws.
They are long, curved, and sharp.
Once they sink in,
they are very hard to pull out.
The frog shakes its head.
It kicks and scrapes at its own skin.
But the larva is small,
and it is holding on at a
place the frog cannot easily reach.
The tongue, the frog's best weapon,
is now useless.
What does the frog do when it
cannot get rid of its attacker?
In some cases, it swallows the larva.
In seven of the trials,
the amphibian gulped the larva
down and later spat it back out, alive.
In one case, a young toad kept
a larva in its stomach for about
two hours before it came back up.
The larva then simply attached
itself to the skin of the animal
that had swallowed it.
The usual rule of the food chain
had failed, again.
Here is what the experiments showed.
The team used 420 larvae and ran
382 encounters with five kinds
of amphibians: a green toad,
a tree frog, a water frog,
a banded newt, and a fire salamander.
One detail matters.
The amphibians were young,
only two to three weeks after metamorphosis.
So these were not giant frogs.
They were small, but still much
bigger than the larvae that beat them.
In about seventy percent of those
encounters, the larva lured the
amphibian before it attacked,
and the amphibian was eaten.
In the rest, the meeting was
accidental, with no luring,
but it still ended badly for the amphibian.
Across the study, the authors report
a success rate of close to one
hundred percent for the larvae.
What happens after the jaws bite?
Like many ground beetle larvae,
Epomis feeds in a way that sounds strange.
It cannot swallow chunks of meat.
So it first sucks out the body
fluids of its victim,
and later it chews.
The press coverage of the study
describes a slow process.
In the end, the researchers report
that all that remains of the
amphibian is a pile of bones.
The slow part matters.
Ground beetle larvae often use
digestive fluids to soften their
food before they take it in.
That lets a tiny animal eat
something far larger than its own mouth.
A larva can stay fixed to one
spot on its host,
feed, and grow, while the amphibian
can do nothing about it.
What we do know is that this
larva has three stages.
At the end of each stage,
it drops off its host and molts
in a hidden place.
Each new stage needs a new meal.
Reports on the study say that a
larva kills just one amphibian
in its first stage,
and as many as nine in its third.
That is a lot of victims for
something so small.
These numbers come from news
summaries of the research,
so treat them as a rough picture,
not a precise count.
After the third stage,
the larva digs into the soil and
builds a small chamber.
Inside, in the dark, it changes.
Its body is taken apart and rebuilt.
Weeks later, an adult beetle comes
out, with a hard shell and long
legs, ready to run across the ground at night.
You might expect the adult to move
on to an easier diet.
Instead, the adult is also a hunter
of amphibians.
The study describes adults as
generalist predators that eat many
kinds of food, including amphibians.
So we cannot say that adult Epomis
eat only frogs.
What we can say is that they
do attack them.
In the laboratory, the researchers
saw an adult jump onto the back
of an amphibian.
It used its jaws to make a
cut in the back,
and the victim became paralyzed
within a few minutes.
Within hours, the adult had eaten
most of its prey,
working from the legs up,
until only a head and limbs were left.
These details come from reports
on the study, and the authors
describe adult hunting as
early-stage research.
The wild observations are even
more interesting.
Wizen and Gasith found three adult
beetles in the wild that were eating
toads from behind.
That fits what we saw in the lab.
But three beetles is a small sample.
Nobody can yet say how often adults
do this outside the laboratory,
or exactly how the bite works.
What about the poison in toads?
Many toads carry defensive chemicals
in their skin.
It would be tempting to say that
Epomis is immune.
But the original paper does not
report on toxin tests.
So the honest answer is that we
do not know how these beetles deal
with toad poison.
No one has solved that puzzle yet.
Why would a beetle ever evolve
such a bold strategy?
Scientists suspect it started as a defense.
If a larva lives where amphibians
hunt, the ones that learned to
dodge a tongue and bite back would survive.
Over a long time,
defense could turn into attack.
This is a hypothesis.
It is a reasonable one,
but it is not a proven history.
There is also a bigger idea behind this story.
Biologists sometimes talk about
the Red Queen hypothesis.
It says that living things keep
changing just to keep up with each
other, like runners on a treadmill.
A frog's hunting reflex works well
against most insects.
That makes the one insect that
can beat it very unusual,
and very interesting.
The frog's weakness is also its strength.
The reflex that finds food quickly
cannot easily stop to ask whether
the target is a worm or a trap.
The same speed that makes frogs
good hunters makes them easy to fool.
Epomis does not beat the reflex with strength.
It beats it with timing and a clever disguise.
Where do these beetles live?
The study was done in Israel,
on two species, Epomis
circumscriptus and Epomis dejeani.
Other species in the genus have
been reported in other parts of
the Old World, including Africa and Asia.
The same paper points to older
reports of another species,
Epomis nigricans, feeding on
amphibians in Japan and in Sri Lanka.
So this habit is not a one-country curiosity.
But the wild lives of most of
these beetles are poorly known,
which is part of why Epomis still
surprises scientists.
It also reminds us how little we
see at night.
These beetles are small,
they hide in shelters during the
day, and they hunt in the dark.
Amphibians use the same damp hiding
places, under stones and old wood.
Adults and amphibians often share
a shelter by day,
and the beetles act at night.
For a very long time,
no one had watched what really
happened between them.
When researchers finally did,
they found a story that nobody expected.
Let us put the whole story together.
A larva waits in the dark and
waves its antennae.
A young amphibian sees a worm and strikes.
The larva slips the tongue and bites on.
It feeds, drops off,
molts, and does it again.
Later it becomes an adult that
can ambush an amphibian by jumping
onto its back.
At no point in this chain is
the beetle stronger than its prey.
It is simply better prepared.
So the next time you stand beside
a quiet pond on a warm evening,
listen to the frogs.
Under the sound is a tiny, patient drama.
Somewhere on the mud,
a small larva may be waving its
antennae, waiting for a much bigger
animal to make one mistake.
It is a lesson about size.
We assume that bigger animals always
win, and that a backbone beats a bug.
Nature does not care about our rankings.
Given enough time, evolution can
find a way to turn almost any
strength into a weakness.
Which other hunters are hiding
a trick we have not noticed yet?
